properties.name: Veleia
properties.one_line: Trajan secured 1,044,000 sesterces in mortgage loans against 46 local estates here, and the 5% interest fed and educated 253 boys and 77 girls of the ager Veleias every month. The bronze tablet recording every loan and every pledged farm, turned up by ploughmen in 1747, is the largest inscribed bronze plaque to survive from the ancient world.
sources: R. Duncan-Jones, 'The Purpose and Organisation of the Alimenta', PBSR 32 (1964)
R. Duncan-Jones, The Economy of the Roman Empire (1974)
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Tabula alimentaria per un prestito ipotecario imperiale, da veleia, II secolo, 01.jpg?width=800
properties.image_credit: Tabula Alimentaria of Veleia, Museo Archeologico Nazionale di Parma — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Circello
properties.one_line: Trajan lent roughly 400,000 sesterces to 51 landowners of this farming community in 101 CE, and the 5% interest fed 286 boys and girls of a population still known by the name of their Ligurian ancestors, deported here two centuries earlier. The bronze ledger recording every loan and every pledged farm was found at the community's forum near modern Circello.
sources: Museo Nazionale Romano — Terme di Diocleziano, Rome
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/The Arch of Trajan, Institutio Alimenta relief, Benevento, Italy - 49866556976.jpg?width=800
properties.image_credit: Institutio Alimenta relief, Arch of Trajan, Benevento — Carole Raddato via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0

properties.name: Ferentino
properties.one_line: The senator Titus Pomponius Bassus, Trajan's first curator of the alimenta, personally set up the child-welfare fund in this Hernican hill town, and the citizens honored him with a bronze tablet of patronage. Ferentino's Roman terraces and gates, raised from massive polygonal blocks, still carry the town above the Via Casilina.
sources: CIL VI 1492 (Tabula patronatus of T. Pomponius Bassus)
properties.image_credit: Approach to the acropolis, Ferentino — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Como
properties.one_line: Pliny the Younger, grown rich in Rome but still Comum's most devoted son, deeded a farm to his hometown and leased it back for an annual payment that funded food and schooling for freeborn boys and girls, copying the mortgage method Trajan used for the state alimenta. He set out the whole arrangement, sums included, in a letter to a friend he was recruiting to do the same.
properties.image_credit: Lake Como from Narro — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Atina
properties.one_line: A local benefactor endowed Atina's own alimentary fund decades before Trajan expanded the program across Italy, and the town kept his memory in stone long after. Perched on a Volscian hilltop above the upper Liri valley, Atina's Roman circuit walls still ring the old acropolis.
sources: R. Duncan-Jones, The Economy of the Roman Empire (1974)

properties.name: Mentana
properties.one_line: Nomentum sits on the short epigraphic list of Italian towns with a confirmed state alimenta fund, a Trajanic welfare grant layered onto a town already known for its wine and for Martial's country villa nearby. Little of Roman Nomentum shows above ground beneath the modern town of Mentana today.
sources: R. Duncan-Jones, 'The Purpose and Organisation of the Alimenta', PBSR 32 (1964)

properties.name: Pesaro
properties.one_line: Pisaurum, a Roman colony on the Adriatic coast road, is named among the Italian towns that ran a state alimenta scheme under Trajan, funded like every other town's by interest on mortgaged farmland. The colony's grid-planned Roman core still lies beneath the streets of central Pesaro.
sources: R. Duncan-Jones, The Economy of the Roman Empire (1974)
properties.image_credit: Piazza del Popolo, Pesaro — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Saturnia
properties.one_line: Saturnia, an old Etruscan town built over sulfur springs in southern Tuscany, is recorded among the Italian communities that drew on Trajan's alimenta fund for its poorer children. Its Roman-era hot springs still cascade over travertine terraces just outside the walls today.
sources: R. Duncan-Jones, The Economy of the Roman Empire (1974)
properties.image_credit: Cascate del Mulino thermal terraces, Saturnia — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Monteu da Po
properties.one_line: Industria, a river-port colony on the Po that traded in Alpine copper and iron, is counted among the towns with a documented Trajanic alimenta fund. Excavated foundations of its temple to Isis and Serapis, proof of the town's trade ties to Egypt, still stand in the fields outside modern Monteu da Po.
sources: R. Duncan-Jones, The Economy of the Roman Empire (1974)
properties.image_credit: Aerial view of the Industria archaeological site — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Formia
properties.one_line: Formiae, a coastal stop on the Appian Way famous for its oyster beds and seaside villas, is documented among the Italian municipalities running Trajan's alimenta program. Cicero owned a villa here and was killed nearby in 43 BCE, a story every Roman visitor to the town already knew.
sources: R. Duncan-Jones, The Economy of the Roman Empire (1974)
properties.image_credit: Formia at sunset from Castellonorato — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Capena
properties.one_line: Capena, a Faliscan town drawn early into Rome's orbit and known for its cult of the goddess Feronia, is named among the Italian communities running Trajan's alimenta program for poor children. The ancient town site lies a few kilometers from the modern hilltop settlement that still carries its name.
sources: R. Duncan-Jones, The Economy of the Roman Empire (1974)

properties.name: Cupramontana
properties.one_line: The children of Cupra Montana who drew Trajan's alimenta grants set up their own inscription honoring the emperor, calling themselves the 'pueri et puellae alimentari Cuprenses Montani.' The Picene hill town, still ringed by the vineyards that give its Verdicchio wine its name, sits above the Esino valley.
properties.image_credit: Verdicchio vines at Cupramontana — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Acqualagna
properties.one_line: Pitinum Mergens, a small hill town on the Via Flaminia in the Candigliano valley, appears in the alimenta record through an inscription once wrongly assigned to neighboring Urbinum before scholars reattributed it here. The Roman settlement's remains lie scattered through the countryside around modern Acqualagna, now better known for its truffles than its ruins.
sources: R. Duncan-Jones, The Economy of the Roman Empire (1974)
properties.image_url: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Acqualagna veduta interna del Passo del Furlo.jpg?width=800
properties.image_credit: Furlo Pass gorge near Acqualagna — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Subiaco
properties.one_line: An inscription raised by the 'pueri et puellae alimentarii' of Sublaqueum records a local branch of the child-welfare program in the Aniene valley above Rome, a town Nero had earlier dammed into a chain of ornamental lakes. The Roman dams that gave the town its name, sub lacu, 'below the lake,' still show along the riverbed today.
properties.image_credit: Subiaco, view toward the Sacro Speco — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Terracina
properties.one_line: The wealthy Tarracina native Caelia Macrina left the town 1,300,000 sesterces in her will: 300,000 for a new public building and 1,000,000 to fund monthly alimenta payments to 100 boys and 100 girls in memory of her son. Her private foundation began in the 150s CE, decades after this snapshot, though it followed a model Trajan had already made famous at Tarracina's neighboring towns.
properties.image_credit: Temple of Jupiter Anxur, Terracina — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Ephesus
properties.one_line: The Ephesian aristocrat Tiberius Claudius Aristion and his wife built this fountain between 102 and 114 CE, channeling water 210 stadia, roughly 24 miles, into a two-story marble facade with a statue of Trajan in the central niche. The building inscription dedicates it to Artemis of Ephesus, to Trajan, and to the city itself.
sources: IvE 424-425 (building inscription of the Nymphaeum Traiani)
properties.image_credit: Nymphaeum of Trajan, Ephesus — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Ephesus
properties.one_line: The equestrian financier Gaius Vibius Salutaris endowed a foundation of 21,500 denarii and 31 gold and silver statuettes in 104 CE, funding a procession that carried images of Artemis, the emperors, and the city itself from the Artemision to the theatre at every major festival. The 568-line inscription recording his gift once covered an entire theatre wall and is now in the British Museum.
sources: G. M. Rogers, The Sacred Identity of Ephesos: Foundation Myths of a Roman City (1991)
properties.image_credit: Great Theatre of Ephesus — Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Citta di Castello
properties.one_line: Pliny the Younger, patron and native benefactor of Tifernum Tiberinum, paid for a temple at his own expense and wrote to Trajan asking permission to add a statue of the deified Nerva beside the older emperors already displayed inside it. His letters describe choosing the site and commissioning the work in his own words.
properties.image_credit: Cathedral facade, Città di Castello — Wikimedia Commons
